0.title: Haggai: Consider Your Ways
0.overview:
Haggai is a builder's book. Two short chapters, four dated messages, delivered in a single autumn, aimed at one problem: God's house was lying in ruins while everyone got on with their own lives.

The setting is 520 BC. The exile is over. Under Cyrus the Persian, the Jews had been allowed home about eighteen years earlier. They had arrived, laid the foundation of a new temple, met opposition, and stopped. Sixteen years later the site was still a ruin, and the community had settled into comfortable resignation: the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD (1:2). Two men lead them: Zerubbabel, the governor and a descendant of David, and Joshua, the high priest. The book of Ezra records that Haggai and Zechariah got the work moving again (Ezra 5:1-2), and the temple was finished four years later.

Haggai's first message is a question: Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins? (1:4). Then twice: Consider your ways. He points to harvests that disappoint and wages that vanish into a bag with holes (1:6), and says God has been speaking through their household accounts. The people obey, God says I am with you (1:13), and within three weeks the building starts.

The second message meets the discouragement that follows. The older people remember Solomon's temple, and this one looks like nothing (2:3). God does not argue with them. He says Be strong three times, tells them to work, promises My Spirit remains in your midst, and adds a staggering word: The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former (2:9).

The third message is a lesson from the priests: holiness does not spread by contact, but uncleanness does (2:11-14). Restarting a building project cannot cleanse a heart. Yet God ends it with a promise given while the barns are still empty: from this day on I will bless you (2:19).

The fourth message is for Zerubbabel alone. God will shake the nations and overturn thrones, and will make this governor of a small province like a signet ring (2:23).

Two warnings keep the book from being misused. First, it is not a prosperity formula. God is dealing with one covenant people about one specific neglected duty, and his point is priority, which Jesus states positively: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt 6:33). Second, the temple is not a church building; the New Testament calls God's people themselves his temple. The principle that carries over is not architecture but priority: what gets our time, our money and our energy first.

Haggai points to Christ at his two great moments. The promise that God will shake the heavens and the earth is taken up in Hebrews, which says that the shaking removes everything that can be shaken so that Christians may know they are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Heb 12:28). And the promise of greater glory was fulfilled when Jesus walked into that very temple: The first temple had been filled with gold; the second was filled, for a few years, by the presence of the Son of God himself, and the peace promised in this place is the peace he made by his cross.

The signet ring is the sweetest detail. God had once said of Zerubbabel's grandfather, the last king of Judah, that even if he were the signet ring on my right hand he would be torn off (Jer 22:24). Here the ring is given back, to the grandson, and the line runs on through him to Joseph and to Jesus (Matt 1:12). God's promises survive exile, ruin and our own delays.

So Haggai speaks to every believer who has let something important slide. It is honest about our favourite excuse, gentle with our discouragement, and confident that God's work in small hands is never small. Consider your ways, it says — and then, I am with you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — This House Lies in Ruins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the second year of Darius the word comes to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest (v. 1). The people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD (v. 2), and God asks, Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins? (vv. 3-4). Consider your ways: they sow much and harvest little, and wages go into a bag with holes (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's house is neglected for the sake of our own comfort, God can make our comforts leak away.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: These people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD." Then the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, "Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest:

Haggai is precisely dated: the second year of the Persian king Darius, which is 520 BC. The exile is over. Cyrus had let the Jews go home about eighteen years earlier, and they had returned, laid the foundation of a new temple, run into opposition, and stopped.

Two men are named, and they represent the two halves of the community's life: Zerubbabel the governor, the civil leader and a descendant of David, and Joshua the high priest. The book of Ezra records that the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, got the work moving again (Ezra 5:1-2).

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: These people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD."

Here is the excuse, and it is beautifully reasonable: the time has not yet come. Not "we refuse", not "we do not believe". Just: not yet. The economy is poor, the opposition is strong, the paperwork is difficult. Later.

Notice also that God calls them These people, not "my people". Delay has put a distance between them.

Most of what God asks of us is not refused outright. It is postponed. The conversation we should have, the giving we mean to start, the sin we intend to deal with: not yet.

Then the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet,

"Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?"

God takes their own word time and turns it round. If there is no time for my house, how is there time for yours?

Paneled houses means finished interiors, wood panelling on the walls, the mark of a comfortable home. Their own building projects had not been postponed at all. They had money and energy; they simply spent both on themselves.

The test is still a useful one. Look not at what we say our priorities are but at where the time and money actually went last year. That is the real list.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways. You have sown much, and harvested little. You eat, but you never have enough; you drink, but you never have your fill. You clothe yourselves, but no one is warm. And he who earns wages does so to put them into a bag with holes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways.

Two words that could change a life: Consider your ways. Literally, set your heart on your roads: stop, look at where you are actually going.

God does not begin with a command to build. He begins by asking them to think. Most of us drift into wrong priorities rather than choosing them, and the first step back is an honest look.

You have sown much, and harvested little. You eat, but you never have enough; you drink, but you never have your fill. You clothe yourselves, but no one is warm. And he who earns wages does so to put them into a bag with holes.

Now the evidence, and every clause is an experience they had all had. Big sowing, small harvest. Meals that do not satisfy. Drinks that do not cheer. Clothes that do not warm. And the unforgettable image: he who earns wages does so to put them into a bag with holes.

Anyone who has watched a salary vanish knows that bag. The car breaks, the boiler fails, the bills rise, and at the end of the month there is nothing to show for it.

God is saying that this was not bad luck. He had been speaking to them through their own finances, and they had not heard it.

A caution is needed here, because this passage is often misused. God is not saying that giving money to a building project guarantees prosperity. He is dealing with a specific people under a specific covenant, and his point is priority, not investment. Jesus put the same principle positively: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt 6:33).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Consider your ways, God says again (v. 7): Go up to the hills and bring wood and build the house, that I may take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified (v. 8). They looked for much and got little, because God blew it away while each man busied himself with his own house (v. 9); so the dew was withheld and drought called on the land (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's glory, not our convenience, is the point of his house — and he governs the weather that funds our harvests.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways. Go up to the hills and bring wood and build the house, that I may take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified, says the LORD. You looked for much, and behold, it came to little. And when you brought it home, I blew it away. Why? declares the LORD of hosts. Because of my house that lies in ruins, while each of you busies himself with his own house. Therefore the heavens above you have withheld the dew, and the earth has withheld its produce. And I have called for a drought on the land and the hills, on the grain, the new wine, the oil, on what the ground brings forth, on man and beast, and on all their labors."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways.

Go up to the hills and bring wood and build the house, that I may take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified, says the LORD.

The second Consider your ways is followed by something practical. Notice how ordinary the instruction is: go to the hills, cut wood, build. God's work usually begins with a task anyone could describe, not with a feeling.

And notice the reason: that I may take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified. The temple was not for their comfort or their national pride. God wanted a house among his people because he intended to be honoured there. Any work we do for God has the same test: is this for his pleasure and glory, or for ours?

You looked for much, and behold, it came to little. And when you brought it home, I blew it away. Why? declares the LORD of hosts. Because of my house that lies in ruins, while each of you busies himself with his own house.

I blew it away. God takes responsibility for the disappointing harvests. This is uncomfortable, and it is meant to be. He would rather have his people poor and attentive than prosperous and indifferent.

The diagnosis is in the last clause: each of you busies himself with his own house. Not one grand act of rebellion. Everyone simply attending to their own affairs, and nobody attending to God's.

Therefore the heavens above you have withheld the dew, and the earth has withheld its produce.

And I have called for a drought on the land and the hills, on the grain, the new wine, the oil, on what the ground brings forth, on man and beast, and on all their labors."

God says he called for a drought, as a master calls a servant. The list is thorough: grain, wine, oil, crops, livestock, work itself.

We should be careful not to read every hardship as a specific judgment; Job's friends made that mistake, and Jesus corrected it. But we should also not assume that God never speaks through circumstances. Here he says plainly that he did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people obeyed the voice of the LORD their God, and the people feared the LORD (v. 12). Then comes the shortest, best message in the book: I am with you, declares the LORD (v. 13). God stirred up the spirit of leaders and people alike, and within three weeks they were at work (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience brings God's presence, and God himself supplies the will to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the LORD their God had sent him. And the people feared the LORD. Then Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, spoke to the people with the LORD's message, "I am with you, declares the LORD." And the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and worked on the house of the LORD of hosts, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the LORD their God had sent him. And the people feared the LORD.

And now something rare in the prophets: people listen. Haggai preached one short sermon, and the governor, the high priest and all the remnant of the people obeyed. No argument, no delegation to study the matter.

Note the order: they obeyed the voice of the LORD and then the people feared the LORD. Obedience deepened their reverence. We often wait to feel more before we act; doing what God says is frequently the road to feeling rightly about him.

Notice too that God calls them the remnant. This was a small, poor community with a half-built temple, and they were the people of God in the world at that moment.

Then Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, spoke to the people with the LORD's message, "I am with you, declares the LORD."

Four words, and they are the reward of obedience: I am with you. Not "I will make you successful" or "the work will be easy". Something better.

This is the promise God keeps making through the Bible, and it reaches its end in the words of Jesus: behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20). The presence of God is the reward of obedience and the strength for it.

And the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and worked on the house of the LORD of hosts, their God,

Look carefully at who does what. The people obeyed, and it was a real decision for which they were responsible. And the LORD stirred up the spirit of every one of them. Scripture holds both together without embarrassment: God works in his people, and his people work.

That is enormously freeing for anyone who feels no enthusiasm for a duty they know is right. The willingness itself can be asked for.

on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king.

The sermon came on the first day of the month (v. 1); the building began on the twenty-fourth. Twenty-three days from conviction to action, including gathering the materials. After sixteen years of "not yet", three weeks.

1.title: Consider Your Ways
1.overview:
In the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD comes through Haggai to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest (v. 1). The people are saying that the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD, and God asks whether it is time for them to live in panelled houses while his house lies in ruins (vv. 2-4). Twice he says, "Consider your ways": they have sown much and harvested little, eaten without being satisfied and earned wages only to put them in a bag with holes (vv. 5-7).

He tells them to go to the hills, bring wood and build the house, so that he may take pleasure in it and be glorified. They looked for much and it came to little, because he blew it away while each of them busied himself with his own house; so the heavens withheld the dew and he called for a drought on grain, wine, oil, man, beast and all their labour (vv. 8-11).

Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the remnant of the people obey the voice of the LORD and fear him (v. 12). Haggai brings the LORD's message: "I am with you" (v. 13). The LORD stirs up the spirit of the leaders and of all the people, and on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month they come and work on the house of the LORD (vv. 14-15).
1.theology:
Most disobedience is postponement rather than refusal: "the time has not yet come" (v. 2).

Our real priorities are shown by where our time and money actually go (v. 4).

God calls his people to stop and consider the direction of their lives before he tells them what to do (vv. 5, 7).

God may speak through frustrated circumstances, though not every hardship is a specific judgment (vv. 6, 9-11).

God's house exists for his pleasure and glory, not for our convenience (v. 8).

Obedience leads to reverence rather than always following it (v. 12).

God's promise to the obedient is his presence, which is also their strength (v. 13; Matt 28:20).

God stirs up the will of his people, and his people genuinely act (v. 14).
1.examples:
A building site left standing for sixteen years.

Panelled walls at home and rubble at the temple.

A month's wages dropped into a bag with holes in it.

God calling for a drought the way a master calls a servant.

One short sermon, and a whole community obeys it.

Four words as the reward for obedience: I am with you.

Twenty-three days from conviction to the first load of timber.

How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?<sup>4</sup>Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua, son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work, for I am with you, declares the LORD of hosts,<sup>5</sup>according to the covenant that I made with you when you came out of Egypt. My Spirit remains in your midst. Fear not.<sup>6</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land.<sup>7</sup>And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>8</sup>The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts.<sup>9</sup>The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the LORD of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of hosts.'"<sup>10</sup>On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came by Haggai the prophet,<sup>11</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Ask the priests about the law:<sup>12</sup>'If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment and touches with his fold bread or stew or wine or oil or any kind of food, does it become holy?'" The priests answered and said, "No."<sup>13</sup>Then Haggai said, "If someone who is unclean by contact with a dead body touches any of these, does it become unclean?" The priests answered and said, "It does become unclean."<sup>14</sup>Then Haggai answered and said, "So is it with this people, and with this nation before me, declares the LORD, and so with every work of their hands. And what they offer there is unclean.<sup>15</sup>Now then, consider from this day onward. Before stone was placed upon stone in the temple of the LORD,<sup>16</sup>how did you fare? When one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were but ten. When one came to the wine vat to draw fifty measures, there were but twenty.<sup>17</sup>I struck you and all the products of your toil with blight and with mildew and with hail, yet you did not turn to me, declares the LORD.<sup>18</sup>Consider from this day onward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month. Since the day that the foundation of the LORD's temple was laid, consider:<sup>19</sup>Is the seed yet in the barn? Indeed, the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have yielded nothing. But from this day on I will bless you."<sup>20</sup>The word of the LORD came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month,<sup>21</sup>"Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying, I am about to shake the heavens and the earth,<sup>22</sup>and to overthrow the throne of kingdoms. I am about to destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations, and overthrow the chariots and their riders. And the horses and their riders shall go down, every one by the sword of his brother.<sup>23</sup>On that day, declares the LORD of hosts, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of hosts."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Be Strong, for I Am with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A month later God asks the older men who remembered Solomon's temple, How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes? (vv. 1-3). Three times he says Be strong, and adds, Work, for I am with you, and My Spirit remains in your midst. Fear not (vv. 4-5). He will shake all nations and fill the house with glory, for the silver and gold are his: The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God meets discouragement over small beginnings with his presence, his Spirit and a promise of greater glory.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet: "Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people, and say, 'Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet:

"Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people, and say,

'Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?

Work has been going for about a month, and the excitement has worn off. God asks a question aimed at the oldest people in the crowd. Solomon's temple had been destroyed sixty-six years earlier, so a few men in their seventies and eighties could remember it: the gold, the scale, the glory. Ezra records that when the foundation of this new temple was laid, those same old men wept with a loud voice (Ezra 3:12).

Is it not as nothing in your eyes? God does not argue with their disappointment. He states it. The new building genuinely was a poor thing compared with what had stood there.

Every church that remembers better days knows this feeling, and so does every believer whose present walk with God seems thin compared with an earlier season. God's answer is not to deny the comparison.

Comparison is a thief. It can be honest and still leave us paralysed, and God's way of dealing with it here is not to talk the people out of their memory but to give them something better to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua, son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work, for I am with you, declares the LORD of hosts, according to the covenant that I made with you when you came out of Egypt. My Spirit remains in your midst. Fear not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua, son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work, for I am with you, declares the LORD of hosts,

Three times, to three groups: Be strong. The governor needs it, the high priest needs it, and so does every ordinary person on the site.

Then the command that follows courage: Work. Not "wait for better circumstances" or "pray for enthusiasm", but carry on with the job in front of you. And the reason, repeated from 1:13: for I am with you.

according to the covenant that I made with you when you came out of Egypt. My Spirit remains in your midst. Fear not.

The ground of it all is the covenant God made at the exodus, a thousand years before. God's commitments do not expire.

And there is more: My Spirit remains in your midst. The little community had no ark, no visible glory and a half-built temple, but they had the Spirit of God. Zechariah, preaching alongside Haggai, put it memorably to the same governor: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (Zech 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts. The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts. The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the LORD of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of hosts.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land.

And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts.

God lifts their eyes from the scaffolding to the end of history. He will shake everything: heavens, earth, sea, dry land, and all nations.

Hebrews quotes this promise and draws out its meaning: the shaking indicates the removal of things that are shaken, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain, and Christians are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Heb 12:27-28). Everything that can be lost will eventually be lost. What remains is God's kingdom, and his people belong to it.

The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts.

A word for a congregation with no money. They were looking at a small budget; God reminds them that all the silver and gold in the world is already his. He has never been short of funds, only of willing hands.

The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the LORD of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of hosts.'"

How could this shabby building ever be more glorious than Solomon's? In the simplest sense, the temple was later expanded and beautified on a grand scale by Herod, and the wealth of nations did flow into it.

But the real answer is a person. Malachi promised that the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple (Mal 3:1), and he did. Jesus Christ walked in these courts, taught here, and drove out the traders. Solomon's temple had gold; this one had God in the flesh standing in it. And the promise in this place I will give peace came true in him: he himself is our peace (Eph 2:14), and angels sang of peace at his birth (Luke 2:14).

Any believer discouraged by small beginnings should sit with this. The people building that unimpressive temple had no idea what would one day stand inside it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — Holy, Unclean, and Blessed from This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Haggai puts two questions to the priests: holy meat does not make other food holy, but a corpse makes what it touches unclean (vv. 10-13). So it is with this people and their offerings (v. 14). Consider from this day onward: before the foundation was laid, harvests failed and God struck them, yet you did not turn to me (vv. 15-17). Now that the work has begun, though the barns are still empty, from this day on I will bless you (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness is not caught by contact with holy things; but God blesses from the day his people begin to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came by Haggai the prophet, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Ask the priests about the law: 'If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment and touches with his fold bread or stew or wine or oil or any kind of food, does it become holy?'" The priests answered and said, "No." Then Haggai said, "If someone who is unclean by contact with a dead body touches any of these, does it become unclean?" The priests answered and said, "It does become unclean." Then Haggai answered and said, "So is it with this people, and with this nation before me, declares the LORD, and so with every work of their hands. And what they offer there is unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came by Haggai the prophet,

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Ask the priests about the law:

'If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment and touches with his fold bread or stew or wine or oil or any kind of food, does it become holy?'" The priests answered and said, "No."

Then Haggai said, "If someone who is unclean by contact with a dead body touches any of these, does it become unclean?" The priests answered and said, "It does become unclean."

Haggai does something unusual: he asks the priests two technical questions about the law, and they answer correctly.

The first: does holiness spread by contact? If a man carries consecrated meat in his robe and the robe brushes some bread, is the bread now holy? No. The second: does uncleanness spread? If a man who has touched a corpse touches food, is the food unclean? It does become unclean (Num 19:22).

There is the lesson, and it is a sober one. Uncleanness is contagious; holiness is not. Touching holy things does not make anyone holy.

Then Haggai answered and said, "So is it with this people, and with this nation before me, declares the LORD, and so with every work of their hands. And what they offer there is unclean.

Now the application, and it is not what we might expect from a prophet who has just got the temple started. Merely restarting the building does not make them clean. Sixteen years of neglect had left a deeper problem than an unfinished wall, and religious activity cannot scrub it out.

And that is exactly what makes the gospel astonishing. Under the law, the clean thing could not cleanse the unclean; the unclean defiled the clean. Then Jesus put out his hand and touched a leper, and the leper was made clean and Jesus was not defiled. In him the flow runs the other way, because he is not merely holy but the source of holiness.

Two cautions are needed. This is not an argument for avoiding contact with people who do not know God; Jesus touched lepers and ate with sinners, and in him holiness proved stronger than defilement. And it is not a reason to despair, because the very next verses promise blessing. The point is that we cannot make ourselves acceptable by handling sacred things. Church attendance, communion, service on a rota: none of these transfers holiness. Only God can make a person clean, which is why Christ came.

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, consider from this day onward. Before stone was placed upon stone in the temple of the LORD, how did you fare? When one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were but ten. When one came to the wine vat to draw fifty measures, there were but twenty. I struck you and all the products of your toil with blight and with mildew and with hail, yet you did not turn to me, declares the LORD. Consider from this day onward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month. Since the day that the foundation of the LORD's temple was laid, consider: Is the seed yet in the barn? Indeed, the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have yielded nothing. But from this day on I will bless you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now then, consider from this day onward. Before stone was placed upon stone in the temple of the LORD,

how did you fare? When one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were but ten. When one came to the wine vat to draw fifty measures, there were but twenty.

Again the call to consider (the ESV notes it may read "backward"). God asks them to look honestly at the years of neglect: half the expected grain, less than half the expected wine. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew of verse 16 is difficult and the reading follows the Greek.)

I struck you and all the products of your toil with blight and with mildew and with hail, yet you did not turn to me, declares the LORD.

The saddest line in the book: yet you did not turn to me. Amos used the same refrain five times over Israel (Amos 4:6-11). God's discipline is not an end in itself; it is a summons home, and it is possible to endure it without ever hearing it.

Consider from this day onward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month. Since the day that the foundation of the LORD's temple was laid, consider:

Is the seed yet in the barn? Indeed, the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have yielded nothing. But from this day on I will bless you."

Now the turn, and notice its timing. The barns are still empty. The vine, fig, pomegranate and olive have yielded nothing. Nothing visible has changed at all.

And God says, from this day on I will bless you. The date is given precisely, three months after the work began. The blessing is announced before there is any evidence of it, so that they have to take God at his word.

That is how God usually works with his people. The promise comes first and the harvest later, and in between there is a period of believing an empty barn and a full promise at the same time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will shake the heavens and the earth and overthrow the strength of the kingdoms (vv. 20-22). And to the governor of a tiny province he says, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant ... and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God overturns empires and keeps his promise to David's line through an obscure governor of a ruined city.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month, "Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying, I am about to shake the heavens and the earth, and to overthrow the throne of kingdoms. I am about to destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations, and overthrow the chariots and their riders. And the horses and their riders shall go down, every one by the sword of his brother. On that day, declares the LORD of hosts, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of hosts."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month,

"Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying, I am about to shake the heavens and the earth,

and to overthrow the throne of kingdoms. I am about to destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations, and overthrow the chariots and their riders. And the horses and their riders shall go down, every one by the sword of his brother.

The last message of the book is for one man. Zerubbabel governed a small, poor province under Persian rule, and God tells him what is going to happen to the great powers. He will overthrow the throne of kingdoms, destroy their strength, and bring down the horses and their riders in confusion, every one by the sword of his brother.

Persia looked permanent. Every empire does, until it does not.

On that day, declares the LORD of hosts, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of hosts."

This last verse is richer than it looks. A signet ring carried a man's seal; it was how he signed documents and stamped his authority. It was precious, personal and never lent out (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "the signet ring").

Now hear what God had said a lifetime earlier about Zerubbabel's own grandfather, the last real king of Judah: though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off (Jer 22:24). The royal ring had been pulled off and thrown away. Here God says he will take the grandson of that rejected king and make him like a signet ring again.

That is grace working through the generations, and it is not merely sentimental. Zerubbabel appears in the genealogy of Jesus: Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, and on down the line to Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born (Matt 1:12-16). The promise to David ran through this obscure governor, rebuilding a modest temple in a ruined city, and arrived at Christ.

So the book that began with people saying the time has not yet come ends with God saying I have chosen you. Haggai's whole message is that God comes first, that his presence is the reward of obedience, and that what looks small in our hands is where he is doing his largest work.

2.title: The Latter Glory of This House
2.overview:
A month into the work, God asks who among them saw the former house in its glory, and whether this one seems as nothing in their eyes (vv. 1-3). Three times he says "Be strong", to Zerubbabel, to Joshua and to all the people, and tells them to work, for he is with them according to the covenant made at the exodus; his Spirit remains in their midst, so they need not fear (vv. 4-5). Yet once more he will shake the heavens, earth, sea and dry land, and all nations, so that their treasures come in and he fills this house with glory; the silver and the gold are his, the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, and in this place he will give peace (vv. 6-9).

Three months later Haggai asks the priests two questions from the law: holy meat does not make other food holy, but contact with a corpse does make things unclean. So it is with this people and everything they offer (vv. 10-14). He tells them to consider the years before the foundation was laid, when harvests came to half of what was expected and God struck their work with blight, mildew and hail, and still they did not turn to him (vv. 15-17). Now, from the day the foundation was laid, though the barns are empty and the vine, fig, pomegranate and olive have yielded nothing, God says, "from this day on I will bless you" (vv. 18-19).

A second word comes for Zerubbabel: God is about to shake heaven and earth, overthrow thrones and destroy the strength of the nations, and on that day he will take Zerubbabel his servant and make him like a signet ring, for he has chosen him (vv. 20-23).
2.theology:
God does not deny our disappointment over small beginnings; he answers it with his presence and his promise (vv. 3-5).

Courage and work belong together, grounded in covenant and in the Spirit who remains among God's people (vv. 4-5; Zech 4:6).

Everything that can be shaken will be; only God's kingdom remains (vv. 6-7; Heb 12:26-28).

God owns all the wealth there is; his work is never short of resources, only of willing hands (v. 8).

The glory of the second temple was that Christ stood in it, and the peace promised there is the peace he made (v. 9; Mal 3:1; Eph 2:14).

Holiness is not transferred by contact with holy things; only God can cleanse a person (vv. 11-14; Num 19:22).

God's discipline is a summons home, and it can be endured without being heard (v. 17; Amos 4:6-11).

God announces blessing before there is any evidence of it, so that his people live by his word (vv. 18-19).

God overturns empires and keeps his promise to David's line through obscure people, all the way to Christ (vv. 21-23; Jer 22:24; Matt 1:12).
2.examples:
Old men weeping at a foundation because they remember something better.

"Be strong" said three times to three different people on one building site.

A congregation with no money told that all the gold is God's already.

A shabby temple that would one day have God standing in it.

Two questions to the priests, and a lesson about what is catching.

Empty barns and a promise of blessing given on the same day.

A signet ring torn off a grandfather and given back to a grandson.
